nodes.name: Calf (triceps surae)
nodes.layer: — (§1.2: a parent, neither drawn nor selectable; if the type needs a value, 'mixed', as the forearm's groups use)
nodes.layerEvidence: Its two members lie in two layers: the gastrocnemius at the surface and the soleus under it (statpearls.calf; radiopaedia.gastrocnemius; elsevier.soleus).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The gastrocnemius is at the surface and forms the main bulk of the calf; the soleus lies under it and shows only at its edges (kenhub.gastrocnemius; grays.surface_lower_extremity). The forearm and hips mark their mixed-layer groups 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts) holds gastrocnemius and soleus separately, not the group.
nodes.location: Back of the lower leg, from just above the knee to the heel: the gastrocnemius at the surface and the soleus under it.
nodes.whatItDoes: Points your foot down at the ankle, as when you rise onto your toes, through one shared tendon to the heel (the Achilles tendon).
nodes.shapeNote: Together the gastrocnemius and the soleus make up most of the muscular outline of the calf. The sources give where the two muscles lie, not how much of that outline each forms. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the gastrocnemius and the soleus inside it.
Some references also count the small plantaris muscle in this group; it is not listed here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, lower_leg:lower_leg.triceps_surae.function, is reviewed. The evidence speaks of the calf muscles as a group (statpearls.calf, radiopaedia.triceps_surae, statpearls.gastrocnemius, elsevier.ankle_moment_arms), so the parent has a function claim; it has no node actions.

nodes.name: Gastrocnemius
nodes.layerEvidence: The most superficial muscle at the back of the leg and the main bulk of the calf (kenhub.gastrocnemius); it sits superficial to the soleus (radiopaedia.gastrocnemius).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The surface muscle of the calf and its main bulk (kenhub.gastrocnemius, radiopaedia.gastrocnemius).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts, mapped to the calves region).
nodes.location: Back of the lower leg, at the surface: two heads from the back of the thigh bone just above the knee, joining into one belly that ends in the Achilles tendon on the heel.
nodes.whatItDoes: Points your foot down at the ankle, as when you rise onto your toes, and helps bend your knee. It crosses both joints, and it gives less to pointing the foot when the knee is bent.
nodes.shapeNote: The surface muscle of the calf, so it may contribute most of the calf's upper outline; its inner head is usually the longer and reaches lower. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its two heads are counted as one muscle here: they share their actions.
With the knee bent it contributes less to pointing the foot, but it still works; how the work splits with the soleus also differs between people.

nodes.name: Soleus
nodes.layer: intermediate (surface outcrops, both sides of the calf)
nodes.layerEvidence: It lies immediately deep to the gastrocnemius (kenhub.soleus; elsevier.soleus: 'anterior (deep) to the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius'), above the deep group, which holds the tibialis posterior (statpearls.leg_posterior_compartment). Its edges form curved eminences on either side of the gastrocnemius, the lateral the longer (grays.surface_lower_extremity); it is somewhat wider than the gastrocnemius and projects beyond it at the sides (kenhub.soleus_de). The outcrop note is supported, and the evidence adds that the outer (lateral) outcrop is the longer. Second review: Gray's sentence begins 'At the same time', a condition the excerpt does not show; Kenhub's German article states the projection without one, so the outcrops stand.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Mostly covered by the gastrocnemius; visible only at its edges on either side of it (grays.surface_lower_extremity, kenhub.soleus_de).
nodes.catalogMuscleKeyNote: The §1.2 node key (body-map key) stays soleus. The catalog never tags soleus; catalogMuscleKeyFor in client/src/lib/recordMuscleKeys.ts folds it into calves, and the forearm sets this field to the catalog key (forearms for the brachioradialis), so the catalog key here is calves.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts, mapped to the calves region). 'soleus' is a body-map key, not a catalog key (§1.1); the catalog tags the calf as 'calves'.
nodes.location: Back of the lower leg, under the gastrocnemius, from just below the knee to the Achilles tendon; its edges can show on the inner and outer sides of the calf.
nodes.whatItDoes: Points your foot down at the ankle. It does not cross the knee, so it keeps working when the knee is bent, and it helps hold you upright when you stand.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies mostly under the gastrocnemius, so its own outline can show mainly as curved edges on the inner and outer sides of the calf, the outer one described as the longer. Under the gastrocnemius it may add to the calf's overall thickness. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Bent-knee calf work takes less from the gastrocnemius, but in the studies cited the gastrocnemius was still active then, and the soleus also works with the knee straight.
Some people have an extra (accessory) soleus muscle on the inner side of the lower leg above the ankle.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, lower_leg:lower_leg.soleus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Tibialis anterior
nodes.layerEvidence: Lies superficially and is easily palpable lateral to the anterior border of the tibia (kenhub.tibialis_anterior; teachmeanatomy.tibialis_anterior).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface beside the front edge of the shin bone, easily felt (kenhub.tibialis_anterior, teachmeanatomy.tibialis_anterior); its tendon is the innermost tendon at the front of the ankle (statpearls.tibialis_anterior).
nodes.location: Front of the lower leg, at the surface, just to the outer side of the shin bone's front edge; its tendon crosses the front of the ankle to the inner side of the foot.
nodes.whatItDoes: Pulls the top of your foot up toward the shin, and helps tilt the sole inward. In walking it steadies the ankle as the foot lands and lifts the foot clear of the ground as the leg swings forward.
nodes.shapeNote: At the surface beside the shin bone, so it may contribute to the muscular outline along the front and outer side of the shin. Its tendon at the front of the ankle can be easy to see; a visible tendon is not muscle size. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Other muscles at the front of the shin also pull the foot up; they are not listed here.
References disagree on how much it tilts the sole inward, so that action is counted as help, not a main action.

nodes.name: Fibularis longus and brevis
nodes.layerEvidence: Fibularis longus lies superficially in the lateral compartment and is the larger, more superficial of the two (kenhub.fibularis_longus; teachmeanatomy.lateral_compartment_leg). Fibularis brevis lies deep to the longus (teachmeanatomy.lateral_compartment_leg; statpearls.fibularis_brevis). The node's surface layer is the longus's; the brevis part of the node is under it (see deviation D2).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The longus is at the surface on the outer side of the leg; the brevis lies under it (teachmeanatomy.lateral_compartment_leg, statpearls.fibularis_brevis).
nodes.catalogMuscleKeyNote: The §1.2 node key (body-map key) stays peroneals. The catalog has no key for these muscles: catalogMuscleKeyFor in client/src/lib/recordMuscleKeys.ts returns null for peroneals, so the catalog key here is none.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Candidate only: the canonical list holds fibularis_longus and fibularis_brevis separately (both mapped to no region); this node refines both. The database lane decides whether a node may name one of two.
nodes.location: Outer side of the lower leg, along the fibula from below the knee toward the ankle: the longus at the surface and the brevis under it, lower down. Their tendons pass behind the outer ankle bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Tilt the sole of your foot outward, and give a little help pointing the foot down. The longus also helps support the arches of the foot. In everyday movement they mainly help steady the foot and stop the sole turning inward too far.
nodes.shapeNote: The longus lies at the surface on the outer side of the lower leg, so the pair may contribute to the muscular outline there, between the front and the back of the lower leg. The brevis lies under the longus and has little separately visible contour. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Two muscles, fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, are counted here as one: they lie together on the outer side of the leg and share their main action, tilting the sole outward.

nodes.name: Tibialis posterior
nodes.layerEvidence: The deepest muscle of the posterior compartment, lying directly against the posterior tibia (statpearls.tibialis_posterior; teachmeanatomy.posterior_compartment_leg; kenhub.tibialis_posterior); one of the deep group (statpearls.leg_posterior_compartment).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The deepest muscle at the back of the leg, under the calf muscles (statpearls.tibialis_posterior, kenhub.tibialis_posterior).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts, mapped to no region).
nodes.location: Back of the lower leg, deepest layer, against the back of the shin bone; its tendon passes behind the inner ankle bone and fans out under the foot.
nodes.whatItDoes: Tilts the sole of your foot inward and helps point the foot down. It helps hold up the inner arch of the foot, especially as you walk.
nodes.shapeNote: The deepest muscle at the back of the lower leg, under the calf muscles, so it has little or no contour of its own; the shape at the back of the leg comes from the muscles over it, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the calf muscles because of where it sits; lower-leg specialization does not target it.
Tilting the sole inward loads it together with the tibialis anterior.

claims.statement: The calf muscles (triceps surae) are the gastrocnemius, with its two heads, and the soleus under it. Their tendons join in the Achilles tendon, which attaches to the heel bone, and together they point the foot down at the ankle (plantar flexion). In a cadaver study they were, with the long flexor of the big toe, the most important plantar flexors by leverage. One anatomy reference also credits them with a part in tilting the heel inward; in the same cadaver study the direction of their leverage below the ankle changed with the foot's position, so that action is not counted here.

claims.statement: Three studies measured how bending the knee changes the gastrocnemius's part in pointing the foot down. In 10 men, maximal plantar-flexion force fell as the knee bent, and at matched efforts gastrocnemius activity fell with it while soleus activity did not change; the authors estimated that the gastrocnemius gives at least two fifths of the force with the knee straight. In single-leg heel raises by 48 adults, gastrocnemius activity was slightly lower with the knee bent to 45 degrees than with it straight, a change the authors judged might be too small to affect clinical or muscle-specific outcomes. In 30 men pointing the foot against a machine with the knee bent to 90 degrees, force and inner-head activity were each about a third lower than with the knee straight. These are short-term activity measurements, not growth; they support describing the knee angle of a calf exercise, not a fixed split of credit.

claims.statement: Whether turning the toes in or out changes which gastrocnemius head works more is unsettled. In heel raises with a heavy free weight by 20 trained adults, toes turned out made the inner head more active than the outer head, and toes turned in did the reverse. Two smaller studies, heel raises on a leg-press machine by 10 trained men and heel raises seated and standing by 12 students, found no clear effect of turning the feet or legs. None of these measured growth, and the atlas counts the gastrocnemius as one muscle.

claims.statement: The soleus points the foot down at the ankle (plantar flexion). It starts on the shin bone and the fibula just below the knee and joins the gastrocnemius in the Achilles tendon, so it crosses the ankle but not the knee. One anatomy reference describes the two working together with the knee straight and, with the knee bent, the gastrocnemius's part as greatly reduced, so that the soleus acts as a primary plantar flexor. In muscle-activity studies, gastrocnemius activity was slightly lower in heel raises with the knee bent to 45 degrees, and inner-head activity about a third lower in machine efforts with the knee bent to 90 degrees. It also helps hold the body upright in standing. In an imaging study of 12 healthy people, its force-producing cross-section was about three times that of the inner gastrocnemius head and eight times that of the outer head.

claims.statement: The soleus starts just below the knee, so it does not cross the knee. Studies have compared its activity with the gastrocnemius's at different knee angles. In 10 men pushing the foot down at matched efforts, soleus activity stayed the same as the knee bent, while gastrocnemius activity fell. In single-leg heel raises by 48 adults, soleus activity was slightly higher with the knee bent to 45 degrees than with it straight. In 30 men with the knee bent to 90 degrees, soleus activity was higher in the first half of the slower movements. So in all three studies bending the knee lowered gastrocnemius activity, by amounts that differed between studies, while the soleus was active with the knee straight as well. These are short-term activity measurements, not growth, and not a fixed split of credit.

claims.statement: Tibialis anterior is the strongest muscle pulling the top of the foot up toward the shin (dorsiflexion), and it also tilts the sole inward (inversion). nodeActions.evidence: A plantar flexor in every reference (statpearls.gastrocnemius, kenhub.gastrocnemius, teachmeanatomy.posterior_compartment_leg); at least two fifths of plantar-flexion force with the knee straight (pmid.7498381, cited on its selectivity claim).
Its main action (kenhub.soleus, radiopaedia.soleus); described as a primary plantar flexor with the knee bent (kenhub.soleus_video); the largest cross-section of the plantar flexors (pmid.1403308).
The strongest dorsiflexor (statpearls.tibialis_anterior, teachmeanatomy.anterior_compartment_leg); the main dorsiflexor (kenhub.tibialis_anterior).

All references name it (statpearls.tibialis_anterior, kenhub.tibialis_anterior, teachmeanatomy.anterior_compartment_leg), and StatPearls calls it a primary inverter with the tibialis posterior; but two cadaver moment-arm studies gave it less inward leverage than the tibialis posterior: about three fifths of it (pmid.7951975) and about a fifth, with an outward one in some specimens (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms); and Kenhub frames it as the main dorsiflexor that 'also' inverts. Recorded assist on the measured evidence; the claim states the disagreement. Second review: with the second study, assist is a closer call than the lane's draft said; kept assist, and the anatomy lane decides.
nodeActions.productNote: If the page should suggest inversion work for a target muscle, prime here would be a product choice, not the evidence: the only prime inverter on the evidence is the tibialis posterior, an adjacent muscle, whose rows do not drive suggestions.

nodeActions.evidence: Their shared main action (teachmeanatomy.lateral_compartment_leg, kenhub.fibularis_brevis, statpearls.fibularis_longus, statpearls.fibularis_brevis, radiopaedia.fibularis_longus); large and nearly equal eversion leverage (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms).

Named for both by Kenhub and StatPearls and for the longus by TeachMeAnatomy; 'weak' for the longus (radiopaedia.fibularis_longus); 'to a much lesser extent' than the triceps surae by leverage (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms); TeachMeAnatomy lists eversion alone for the brevis.

A primary inverter (statpearls.tibialis_posterior); produces inversion (kenhub.tibialis_posterior; teachmeanatomy.posterior_compartment_leg); the largest inversion moment arm (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms); its large inverter moment arm (biomedcentral.tibialis_posterior_review).
A 'secondary' plantar flexor (statpearls.tibialis_posterior); 'aids' plantar flexion (kenhub.tibialis_posterior); 'to a much lesser extent' by leverage (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms).

nodeActionsOutsideRegion.evidence: 'Assists with knee flexion' (statpearls.gastrocnemius); listed as an action without a qualifier by Kenhub and TeachMeAnatomy; its pull on the knee is greatest with the knee straight and small at 90 degrees (elsevier.gastrocnemius_knee_flexor). Recorded assist on the evidence.
nodeActionsOutsideRegion.why: knee.flexion is a thigh action, not one of the lower leg's (§1.2). The thigh lists the gastrocnemius as an external member for knee flexion; node actions are global and declared by the home region, so the thigh can show it only if the lower leg declares this row. Declared in the lower leg's own nodeActions, it would also reach the lower leg's page, whose test refuses a node action outside the page's actions. Not placed in nodeActions until D1 is decided.

nodeActionsLeftOut.reason: StatPearls credits the triceps surae with a part in subtalar inversion, but the cadaver moment-arm study found the calf's leverage below the ankle changes direction with the foot's position (elsevier.ankle_moment_arms). Said in the calf's function claim; not counted.

As for the gastrocnemius: references credit the triceps surae as a whole, and the measured leverage changes direction with foot position. Second review: a second cadaver study gave the soleus a small inward leverage, about a quarter of the tibialis posterior's (pmid.7951975, cited on the tibialis anterior's function claim); still not counted.
A parent: it acts through the gastrocnemius and soleus, which carry the rows (10-multi-region.md §7.3; the platform exempts parents from the main-action test).

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb, Gastrocnemius Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results (Q1, Q5, Q41): the Bookshelf id NBK532946, the PubMed record 30422541 titled 'Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb, Gastrocnemius Muscle', and statpearls.com mirrors (point-of-care/22091; update shown as April 2026). The excerpts gave: a superficial, biarticular muscle forming the triceps surae with the soleus; origin on the medial and lateral femoral condyles, insertion on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon; one of the plantar flexors that also assists knee flexion; the triceps surae produces plantar flexion and contributes to subtalar inversion; variants include the gastrocnemius tertius. Authors not shown. One summary line said the plantaris is 'present in only a small share of people'; that reads as a misquote (other references describe the plantaris as present in most people and absent in some) and is not used. Second review (SR21): an independent search did not return the NBK532946 article; the lane's results showed its address and PubMed record 30422541. Not confirmed further.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Calf
sources.notes: Seen as statpearls.com point-of-care 24167 and its dev mirrors (Q3, Q4); a summary reported the NCBI Bookshelf id NBK459362, which was not opened. The excerpts gave: the gastrocnemius and soleus are the calf's two largest muscles; the soleus is a large, flat muscle deep to the gastrocnemius; both form the triceps surae and join in the Achilles tendon; the calf muscles plantar flex the ankle and are supplied by the tibial nerve. The statpearls.com page was updated 31 Jan 2026 and the mirrors show 23 May 2023; versions may differ. Authors not shown. Second review (SR21): the NBK459362 id was again seen only by report, not confirmed.

sources.title: Influence of gastrocnemius muscle length on triceps surae torque development and electromyographic activity in man
sources.notes: PubMed record and abstract seen in search results (Q11, Q20): Cresswell, Löscher and Thorstensson, Exp Brain Res 1995;105(2):283-290. Ten men; plantar-flexor torque and surface and intramuscular EMG at knee angles from straight to strongly bent with the ankle angle held; maximal and resting twitch torque fell with knee flexion; at similar effort gastrocnemius EMG RMS fell with knee flexion while soleus RMS was unchanged; gastrocnemius estimated at at least 40 per cent of plantar-flexor torque with the leg straight. Abstract only; full text not seen.

sources.title: Influence of knee flexion angle and age on triceps surae muscle activity during heel raises
sources.notes: PubMed record and abstract seen in search results (Q10, Q12, Q21): Hébert-Losier and colleagues, J Strength Cond Res 2012;26(11):3124-3133. 48 healthy adults in two age groups did single-leg heel raises at 0 and 45 degrees of knee flexion; mean triceps surae activity about 23 and 21 per cent of maximum; soleus about 4 per cent higher and the gastrocnemius heads about 5 per cent lower at 45 degrees; the authors judged the change might not be enough to influence clinical or muscle-specific outcomes; age had no effect. Co-authors beyond Schneiders (named in the query, not in the result) not confirmed. A companion fatigue paper (DOI 10.1519/JSC.0b013e318243ff0e) was not cited.

sources.title: Knee position affects medial gastrocnemius and soleus activation during dynamic plantarflexion: no evidence for an inter-muscle compensation in healthy young adults
sources.notes: Open-access article in Biology Open 2024;13(12), 30 Dec 2024 (also given as 15 Dec in a repository), by Kovács, Csala, Yang, Tihanyi, Gu and Hortobágyi (Q16, Q19, Q22, Q55). Seen through search summaries only. 30 healthy men; concentric plantar flexions at five velocities with the knee straight and at 90 degrees; two 16-channel EMG arrays on the medial gastrocnemius and soleus; torque 31 per cent lower and medial gastrocnemius EMG 35 per cent lower with the knee bent; soleus EMG 15 and 28 per cent higher in the first half of slower contractions with the knee bent; no evidence that soleus activation compensated. PubMed id not shown.

sources.title: Neuromechanical coupling within the human triceps surae and its consequence on individual force-sharing strategies
sources.notes: Crouzier, Lacourpaille, Nordez, Tucker and Hug, J Exp Biol 2018;221(21):jeb187260 (Q54, Q61); seen through an open-archive record, a sports-science catalogue and search summaries. 20 volunteers; isometric plantar flexions; activation of the two gastrocnemius heads and the soleus by EMG and cross-section by imaging; activation and cross-section shares correlated for the two gastrocnemius heads at up to half of maximal effort; the imbalance of force between the three heads varied greatly between participants. PubMed id not shown; the underlying data are deposited in a public data repository. Second review (SR11): an independent search showed the same abstract and authors.

sources.title: Physiological cross-sectional area of human leg muscles based on magnetic resonance imaging
sources.notes: PubMed record and abstract seen in search results (Q50, Q52): Fukunaga and colleagues, J Orthop Res 1992;10(6):928-934 (another record gives pages 926-934, and a repository lists Shellock first; author order not confirmed). MRI of 12 healthy subjects; mean volumes 489, 245 and 140 cm3 for the soleus and the medial and lateral gastrocnemius; soleus cross-section about 230 cm2, roughly three and eight times the two heads'; soleus fibres short for its volume. DOI not shown. Second review (SR20): PubMed shows 928-934 and a Springer reference list 926-934; a JAXA record lists Shellock first. Still unresolved; the numbers cited agree.

sources.title: Moment arm length variations of selected muscles acting on talocrural and subtalar joints during movement: an in vitro study
sources.notes: Klein, Mattys and Rooze, J Biomech 1996;29(1):21-30 (Q46, Q49, Q57); seen through a sports-science catalogue record, a university library record and summaries of the abstract. Tendon-excursion method on 10 anatomical preparations for the triceps surae, flexor hallucis longus, tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior and the two fibularis muscles. Main plantar flexors by moment arm: triceps surae and flexor hallucis longus, and to a much lesser extent the fibularis muscles and tibialis posterior. Subtalar: tibialis posterior the largest inversion moment arm (about -19.1 mm), tibialis anterior very low (about -3.8 mm) and everting in some specimens; the fibularis muscles nearly identical (21.8 and 20.5 mm); the triceps surae inverting in eversion and everting in inversion. PubMed id (8839014 was guessed in a query) not confirmed. Second review (SR15): an independent search confirmed the authors as Klein, Mattys and Rooze (J Biomech 1996;29(1):21-30) and every moment arm quoted here; a secondary review gives 9 specimens for the morphometric data, against the abstract's 10. The same results named a second cadaver study with a different value for the tibialis anterior (pmid.7951975).

sources.title: The function of gastrocnemius as a knee flexor at selected knee and ankle angles
sources.notes: Li, Landin, Grodesky and Myers, J Electromyogr Kinesiol 2002;12(5):385-390 (Q5, Q38); seen through a university repository record and a summary of its abstract. 17 participants on a dynamometer with the gastrocnemius selectively stimulated electrically; the knee-flexion moment was largest with the knee straight at every ankle angle, fell most between 180 and 165 degrees, and was small at 90 and 75 degrees. DOI and PubMed id not shown. Second review (SR13): an independent search confirmed J Electromyogr Kinesiol 2002;12(5):385-390 (October 2002), the 17 participants and the findings quoted; knee angle 180 degrees is straight.

sources.title: Foot movement and tendon excursion: an in vitro study
sources.notes: Added by the second review. PubMed record seen through a generated search summary (SR16): Foot Ankle Int 1994;15(7):386-395. 15 fresh foot-leg specimens in a leg-holding device; inverter moment arms about the foot's eversion-inversion axis relative to the tibialis posterior (1.00): tibialis anterior 0.59, flexor digitorum longus 0.75, flexor hallucis longus 0.62, soleus 0.24; the fibularis longus and brevis negative (-0.82, -0.85), so everters. Authors not shown in the results (the review's query named Hintermann, Nigg and Sommer; not confirmed). Abstract only; full text not seen.

sources.title: Medial and lateral gastrocnemius activation differences during heel-raise exercise with three different foot positions
sources.notes: Riemann, Limbaugh, Eitner and LeFavi, J Strength Cond Res 2011;25(3):634-639 (Q15, Q17, Q56); seen through university repository records and summaries of the abstract. 20 resistance-trained adults; free-weight heel raises on a block at about 1.3 times body mass; surface EMG; toes out gave more medial than lateral gastrocnemius activity in both phases, toes in the reverse; the authors say the study cannot predict training adaptations. PubMed id not shown (21311349 was guessed in a query and not confirmed).

sources.title: Does feet position alter triceps surae EMG record during heel-raise exercises in leg press machine?
sources.notes: Manual Therapy, Posturology & Rehabilitation Journal 2017; first author Reginaldo S. Pereira, with Danilo S. Bocalini among the co-authors (Q18, Q63). 10 trained men aged 20 to 30; heel raises on a 45-degree leg press with neutral, inward and outward foot positions; surface EMG of the soleus and both gastrocnemius heads; no significant interaction between EMG and foot position; soleus values lower than both heads'. The abstract excerpt was cut off; the full results were not seen.

sources.title: Effects of lower extremity rotation on muscle activity during heel-raise exercise
sources.notes: A Nova Southeastern University repository record of a paper in Gazzetta Medica Italiana, vol. 180 (Q66); publisher taken to be Edizioni Minerva Medica, not confirmed. 12 healthy college students; 10 heel raises in neutral, maximal inward and maximal outward leg rotation, seated and standing; rotation did not significantly affect triceps surae activation. Authors, year and DOI not shown.

sources.title: Tibialis posterior in health and disease: a review of structure and function with specific reference to electromyographic studies
sources.notes: Semple, Murley, Woodburn and Turner, J Foot Ankle Res 2009;2:24, open access (Q39, Q65); seen through search summaries. A narrative review of anatomy and EMG studies: the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch in walking; the most powerful supinator of the hindfoot through its large inverter moment arm at the subtalar joint. The PubMed id 19691828 was supplied in a query and the summary said it matched; no PubMed page was shown. One index lists the authors in a different order.

sources.title: The presence of accessory soleus muscle in humans
sources.notes: Einstein (São Paulo) 2012;10(1):79-81; authors per DOAJ Flavio Belmont Del Nero, Cristiane Regina Ruiz and Roberto Aliaga Junior (the journal page renders the names incompletely) (Q36, Q58). 154 ankle MRI scans; accessory soleus in 11.6 per cent (7.8 in men, 15.6 in women); the introduction quotes 0.7 to 5.5 per cent from anatomical studies. Abstract only.

sources.title: Prevalence of the Peroneus Quartus Muscle and Its Association with Peroneal Tendon Pathologies: An MRI Study of 1160 Ankles
sources.notes: Yuksel, Ergun and Kose, Diagnostics 2025;15:2329, published 14 Sep 2025; also PMC12468075 (Q42, Q59). 1160 ankle MRI scans from 1073 patients; peroneus quartus in 123 (10.6 per cent), more in men (12.7) than women (9.2); associated with fibularis brevis tendinitis and longitudinal tears and with fibularis longus tendinitis. Dissection-study rates seen in the same search (5.2 and 21.7 per cent in two series; 6.6 to 23 per cent in a review) could not be traced to a named paper and are not used. Abstract and summaries only.

sources.title: Peroneus quartus muscle: MR imaging features
sources.notes: Radiology, 1 Mar 1997 (Q42, Q59); the result showed only the date as its title, and the title here is descriptive, after an index entry 'PERONEUS QUARTUS MUSCLE - MR-IMAGING FEATURES' that may be the same paper. 136 consecutive ankle MRIs; prevalence 10 per cent (14 cases); insertion varied, the calcaneus the most common site. Authors and PubMed id not shown. Second review (SR12): an independent search showed the title 'Peroneus quartus muscle: MR imaging features', by Cheung and colleagues, Radiology 1997;202(3):745-750, and the 14 of 136 ankles; the title above now drops the descriptive '(Radiology, 1997)'. The full author list and PubMed id were still not shown.

sources.title: Prevalence and morphology of the gastrocnemius tertius: anatomical study and literature review
sources.notes: Triantafyllou, Zielinska, Piagkou, Koptas, Węgiel and Olewnik, published 28 Mar 2025 (Q45, Q60). 73 lower limbs from a Central European cadaver sample: a third head in 8 (10.96 per cent), six fused with the lateral head and two with the medial; pooled prevalence 4.34 per cent from a literature meta-analysis. The journal is inferred from the DOI prefix (Surgical and Radiologic Anatomy), not shown. Abstract and summaries only.

sources.title: Topography of the gastrocnemius heads in 32 cadaveric legs (Keimyung University repository record, 2024)
sources.notes: A Keimyung University medical library repository record, August 2024 (Q53, Q64). The title here is descriptive: the record's title, authors and journal were not shown (a summary guessed Anatomy & Cell Biology; not confirmed). 32 cadaveric legs: the medial head longer than the lateral in 28; muscle-tendon junctions about 152 mm (medial) and 175 mm (lateral) above the calcaneal tuberosity, the lateral higher in 25 legs; the abstract notes the muscle's form matters for calf shape.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: The Posterior Compartment of the Leg
sources.notes: Seen through search excerpts (Q31); the excerpt was cut off before the soleus, plantaris and tibialis posterior sections of the English page, and the tibialis posterior lines may come from the same site's encyclopaedia or Spanish page. The excerpts gave: seven muscles in superficial and deep groups acting to plantar flex and invert the foot; the gastrocnemius's two heads from the femoral condyles, plantar flexion at the ankle and flexion at the knee; the tibialis posterior the deepest muscle, directly against the posterior tibia, plantar flexing and inverting the foot; all supplied by the tibial nerve. Title follows the page's subject; exact heading not shown.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: Muscles in the Anterior Compartment of the Leg
sources.notes: Seen through search excerpts (Q23, Q32): a group of four muscles that dorsiflex and invert the foot, supplied by the deep fibular nerve and the anterior tibial artery; the tibialis anterior's actions are dorsiflexion and inversion; 'a separate TeachMeAnatomy article describes it as the strongest dorsiflexor of the foot' (which article was not shown).

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy encyclopaedia: Tibialis Anterior
sources.notes: Seen through a search summary (Q32): it can be palpated just lateral to the shaft of the tibia; origin on the lateral tibial surface, insertion on the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal; dorsiflexion and inversion.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: The Lateral Compartment of the Leg
sources.notes: Seen through search excerpts (Q30): the common function is eversion; both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve; fibularis longus the larger, more superficial of the two, everting and plantar flexing the foot and supporting the lateral and transverse arches; fibularis brevis deep to the longus, inserting on the fifth metatarsal, with eversion as its only listed action; from the anatomical position only a few degrees of eversion are possible, and in everyday movement the muscles mainly fix the medial margin of the foot in running and prevent excessive inversion. Some lines may come from the site's encyclopaedia entries for the two muscles.

sources.title: Gray's Anatomy of the Human Body (1918), Surface Anatomy of the Lower Extremity (quoted on Wordnik)
sources.notes: The 20th US edition of Gray's Anatomy (1918), public domain, quoted on a Wordnik page tagged chapter XII, section 13 (Q33, Q34). Quoted lines: 'the prominent fleshy mass of the calf of the leg produced by Gastrocnemius and Soleus (Fig. 1239)' and 'the edges of Soleus can be seen forming, on either side of Gastrocnemius, curved eminences, of which the lateral is the longer.' A third-party transcription; the Bartleby edition was not seen, and fidelity was not checked. Second review (SR5, SR7): the quoted soleus sentence begins 'At the same time', so it describes a condition set by the sentence before it, which neither the lane's searches nor the review's showed; a 'stand on tiptoe' line in the same results belongs to a different book (Blaisdell, A Practical Physiology), not Gray's.

sources.title: Kenhub: Gastrocnemius muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a generated search summary (Q8, Q41): the main bulk of the calf and the most superficial posterior leg muscle, forming the triceps surae with the soleus; the medial head from the popliteal surface and posterior medial condyle, the lateral head from the lateral femoral condyle, both also from the knee capsule; both into the calcaneal tendon; actions foot plantar flexion at the talocrural joint and leg flexion at the knee joint; tibial nerve. Authors and update date not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub video: Gastrocnemius muscle functions (3D)
sources.notes: Seen only through a search summary of its transcript (Q8): the medial head is the larger of the two and extends further down the leg. The video was not watched.

sources.title: Kenhub: Soleus muscle
sources.notes: Seen through generated search summaries (Q2, Q7, Q51): origin from the soleal line, the medial border of the tibia and the head and posterior border of the fibula, some fibres from a tendinous arch; merges with the gastrocnemius into the tendon on the posterior calcaneus; main action plantar flexion at the talocrural joint; an antigravity muscle supporting upright posture; runs from just below the knee to the heel, immediately deep to the gastrocnemius; tibial nerve S1-S2. A summary line about the knee-flexed role was the tool's own knowledge, not this page, and was not used.

sources.title: Kenhub: Musculus soleus (German)
sources.notes: German-language Kenhub article seen through a search excerpt (Q35): 'soleus verläuft vertikal unterhalb des M. gastrocnemius entlang des Unterschenkels. Er ist etwas breiter und überragt diesen an den Seiten.' (it runs below the gastrocnemius down the leg, is somewhat wider and projects beyond it at the sides). The English article's wording on this point was not seen.

sources.title: Kenhub video: Soleus muscle (3D)
sources.notes: Seen only through a search summary of its transcript (Q37, Q40): with the knee extended the gastrocnemius and soleus work together as a powerful plantar flexor; with the knee flexed the gastrocnemius's role is greatly reduced and the soleus acts as a primary plantar flexor; the soleus helps keep the body upright in standing. The video was not watched. Second review (SR14): no reputable reference in an independent search restated this; only exercise and coaching sites did (not citable), so the claim attributes it to this one reference.

sources.title: Kenhub: Tibialis anterior muscle
sources.notes: Seen through generated search summaries (Q23, Q44): dorsiflexes the foot at the talocrural joint and inverts it at the subtalar joint ('the main foot dorsiflexor ... but it also inverses the foot'); steadies the ankle at foot strike and lifts the foot during swing; helps support the medial longitudinal arch; lying superficially and easily palpable lateral to the anterior border of the tibia; a cord-like tendon from the distal third of the tibia; deep fibular nerve L4-L5.

sources.title: Kenhub: Tibialis posterior muscle
sources.notes: Seen through generated search summaries (Q25, Q26): the most central and deepest muscle of the posterior leg, one of the deep group with the popliteus and the long toe flexors; aids plantar flexion at the ankle and produces inversion at the subtalar joint, as a synergist of the tibialis anterior; its tendon runs behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel. The German pages call the subtalar action supination.

sources.title: Kenhub: Fibularis (peroneus) longus muscle
sources.notes: Seen through generated search summaries (Q27, Q47): a long muscle located superficially in the lateral compartment with the fibularis brevis; from the upper fibula to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal; its tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus with the brevis's; eversion and plantar flexion; superficial fibular nerve. Nothing on surface palpation was shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: Fibularis brevis muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a generated search summary (Q28): besides plantar flexing the foot, the fibularis brevis and longus also evert it; the brevis inserts on the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal; superficial fibular nerve L5-S1.

sources.title: Kenhub: Fibular (peroneal) muscles of the leg
sources.notes: Kenhub's overview of the two muscles, seen through a generated search summary (Q28, Q47): they make up the lateral compartment; the fibularis longus provides support to the arches of the foot (a German page adds that its tendon braces the transverse arch).

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy: Soleus muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q35): the soleus lies 'anterior (deep) to the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius muscle and the tendon of the plantaris muscle'; it cannot be tested in isolation, so the triceps surae is tested together by resisted plantar flexion. sources.title: Radiopaedia: Triceps surae muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q9): 'Triceps surae muscle is another term used for the calf muscles, more specifically two of the three muscles of the superficial posterior compartment of the leg' (the two heads of the gastrocnemius and the soleus). Authors and revision date not shown.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Soleus muscle
sources.notes: Seen as the images.radiopaedia.org copy through a search excerpt (Q9, Q36): inserts via the tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon) into the mid-posterior calcaneus; plantar flexion; tibial nerve; notes the accessory soleus range of 0.7 to 5.5 per cent, most often on one side. Authors and revision date not shown.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Gastrocnemius muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q41): one of the calf muscles (triceps surae) in the superficial posterior compartment, sitting superficial to the much larger soleus; variants include a fabella, commonly in the lateral head. Its action section was not in the excerpt.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Third head of gastrocnemius
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q45): a normal variant, an accessory muscle bundle in addition to the medial and lateral heads; estimated in 2.0 to 5.5 per cent of the population; most cases asymptomatic, some compressing the popliteal vessels (popliteal artery entrapment). Authors not shown.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Accessory soleus muscle
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q36): uncommon, about 3 per cent (0.7 to 5.5); usually one-sided; a soft mass in the posteromedial distal third of the leg that tends to enlarge with activity, especially plantar flexion; pain common in symptomatic cases. Authors not shown.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Accessory peroneal muscles
sources.notes: Seen through a search excerpt (Q67): the peroneus quartus is a supernumerary muscle of the lateral compartment arising from the distal lateral fibula and descending medial and posterior to the fibularis tendons; its insertion varies (the retrotrochlear eminence of the calcaneus, the fifth metatarsal, the fibularis tendons, the lateral retinaculum or the cuboid); occasionally it crowds the retromalleolar groove, predisposing to fibularis brevis tendon wear and tear. A German reference in the same results (DocCheck Flexikon, user-edited, not cited) gives a different origin. Authors not shown.

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Fibularis longus muscle
sources.notes: Seen as the images.radiopaedia.org copy through a search summary (Q27, Q48): one of the muscles of the lateral compartment; origin the fibular head, insertion the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform; superficial peroneal nerve; main action eversion, with weak plantar flexion. disagreementsAndWording: Straight-knee versus bent-knee calf work. The three studies agree in direction and differ in size: in static efforts at matched levels the gastrocnemius's activity fell with knee flexion and the soleus's did not change (pmid.7498381); in heel raises at 45 degrees the shift was small, about the same size in both directions, and the authors doubted it mattered (pmid.22190157); at 90 degrees in concentric efforts inner-head activity and force were about a third lower, and the soleus rose in the first half of slower movements (biologists.knee_position_plantarflexion). The claims say what each measured, on both nodes, and say that this supports describing knee angle, not a fixed split of credit. Kenhub's video states the textbook position (with the knee bent the soleus becomes the main plantar flexor); it is cited on the soleus's function claim, with the measured nuance on the selectivity claims.

Studies not cited on the knee-angle claims: Signorile et al. 2002 (J Strength Cond Res 16(3):433-439; Q10) reported, per a truncated catalogue abstract, lower soleus activity with the knee straight than bent and no difference between the outer gastrocnemius head and the soleus at any angle; the excerpt was cut off and its methods not seen, so it is not cited. A KoreaScience study of 20 people (gastrocnemius activity changed from 30 degrees of knee flexion, the soleus did not; Q14, Q16) had no title, authors or year in the results, so it is not cited. Both point the same way as the cited studies. Arampatzis et al. 2006 (Q13) attributed the fall in gastrocnemius activity at strongly bent knees to the force-length state of all three muscles; not cited, since its journal was not shown.

Turning the toes in or out (gastrocnemius heads): one study found a clear difference between heads (lww.heel_raise_foot_position), two smaller ones found no effect (mtprehab.heel_raise_leg_press, minerva.heel_raise_leg_rotation); the claim says the question is unsettled and the atlas counts one gastrocnemius.

Tibialis anterior and inversion: StatPearls calls it primarily responsible for dorsiflexion and inversion and a primary inverter with the tibialis posterior; Kenhub calls it the main dorsiflexor that also inverts; a cadaver moment-arm study gave it about a fifth of the tibialis posterior's inversion leverage, everting in some specimens. The claim states the disagreement; the node action is assist on the measured evidence.

Fibularis and plantar flexion: named for both muscles by Kenhub and StatPearls; 'weak' for the longus by Radiopaedia (a Radiopaedia case discussion, not cited, calls it a main action); TeachMeAnatomy lists eversion alone for the brevis; 'to a much lesser extent' than the triceps surae by moment arm. The claim says 'only a little' and names the disagreement; the node action is assist.

Tibialis posterior and plantar flexion: StatPearls uses both 'primarily' and 'secondary'; Kenhub 'aids'; the moment-arm study 'to a much lesser extent'. The claim says it helps; the node action is assist.

The triceps surae and inversion: StatPearls credits a contribution to subtalar inversion; the moment-arm study found the calf's subtalar leverage reverses with foot position. Said in the calf's function claim and kept out of the node actions.

Gastrocnemius head length: the Kenhub video and a 32-leg cadaver study (medial longer in 28) agree that the inner head is usually the longer and reaches lower; the same study found the outer muscle-tendon junction higher in 25 of 32 legs, consistent with that. The appearance claim says 'usually'.

Soleus size: Radiopaedia calls the soleus 'much larger' than the gastrocnemius, while Kenhub calls the gastrocnemius 'the main bulk of the calf'. Both hold (the soleus is the larger by volume and cross-section, pmid.1403308; the gastrocnemius is the visible bulk). The appearance claims say the gastrocnemius forms the main bulk at the surface and the soleus adds thickness under it.

A StatPearls summary line said the plantaris is 'present in only a small share of people'. This looks like a misquote and is not used; the calf's caveat says only that some references count the plantaris in the group.

Second review, soleus compensation at 90 degrees (SR3, SR4): Kovács et al. 2024 found no evidence that soleus activation made up for the medial gastrocnemius's lower activity; a later study of 17 men by some of the same authors (Ye et al., Physiology International 2025;112(3):369-379; seen through a repository listing and a summary, not cited) suggested the soleus may compensate at low speeds. The soleus selectivity claim now says neither.

Second review, tibialis anterior and inversion (SR15, SR16): a second cadaver study (pmid.7951975, 15 specimens) gave the tibialis anterior about three fifths of the tibialis posterior's inverter leverage, against about a fifth in Klein et al.; the claim now gives both, and the node action stays assist as a closer call.

Second review, foot position and the gastrocnemius heads (SR22, SR24, SR26): a further EMG study of 33 young adults (PubMed 28515978; title not shown, not cited) found toes turned out made the inner head more active and toes turned in made no difference between the heads; another, on IOS Press, matched the cited free-weight study's pattern. With the leg-press and seated studies finding no effect, 'unsettled' stands.

Second review, the soleus's outcrops (SR5, SR7): Gray's sentence begins 'At the same time', and the condition it refers to was not found; the soleus appearance claim and node text say the edges 'can' show, and the outward projection rests first on Kenhub's German article.

Second review, the soleus with the knee bent (SR14): independent results restating that the soleus becomes the main plantar flexor with the knee bent came only from exercise and coaching sites, one of which called the mechanism plausible but not firmly established; the soleus function claim attributes the statement to one anatomy reference and adds what two studies measured.

No target muscle of the lower leg is prime for foot.inversion on the recorded evidence: the tibialis anterior is assist, and the only prime inverter is the tibialis posterior, an adjacent muscle whose rows do not drive suggestions. layerAndOutcropChecks: lower_leg.soleus 'intermediate (surface outcrops, both sides of the calf)': supported. Immediately deep to the gastrocnemius (kenhub.soleus, elsevier.soleus) and above the deep group (statpearls.leg_posterior_compartment). StatPearls and TeachMeAnatomy place it in the 'superficial group' of the posterior compartment; that is the compartment's grouping (the soleus with the gastrocnemius and plantaris, against the deep group), not a contradiction of the drawing's middle layer. Outcrops on both sides: Gray's 1918 ('on either side of Gastrocnemius, curved eminences, of which the lateral is the longer') and Kenhub's German article ('etwas breiter und überragt diesen an den Seiten'). The evidence adds that the outer outcrop is the longer: a note for the drawing lane, not a deviation.

secondReview.method: Every reviewed claim was read sentence by sentence against the excerpts recorded in citations[].
